strategies.name: 200-Day Trend Filter
strategies.tagline: Is the stock in a long-term uptrend or downtrend?
how: The 200-day moving average is the average closing price of the last 200 trading days, roughly ten months. Because it moves slowly, it shows the long-term direction and ignores day-to-day noise.
Many investors and funds treat it as a dividing line: above it the stock is in a long-term uptrend, below it in a long-term downtrend. Crossing that line is a change of regime worth knowing about.
strategies.bullish: The stock closes above its 200-day average after closing below it the day before.
strategies.bearish: The stock closes below its 200-day average after closing above it the day before.
strategies.why: Trends tend to persist. Staying on the right side of the long-term average historically avoided most of the deepest drawdowns, because big bear markets spend most of their time below it.
watch_out: In sideways markets the price can cross back and forth many times ("whipsaws"), giving several false alerts in a row.
It reacts late by design: by the time the cross happens, part of the move is already over.
Works better as a filter ("only look at stocks above their 200-day") than as a precise entry point.
strategies.settings: Simple moving average, 200 days, daily closes.

strategies.name: Bollinger Band Reversion
strategies.tagline: Spots stretched moves that are starting to snap back.
how: Bollinger Bands draw an envelope around a 20-day average. The upper and lower bands sit 2 standard deviations away, so they widen when the stock is volatile and tighten when it is calm.
About 95% of closes normally land inside the bands. A close outside is unusual, and the moment the price closes back inside suggests the extreme move is fading.
strategies.bullish: After closing below the lower band, the stock closes back above it.
strategies.bearish: After closing above the upper band, the stock closes back below it.
strategies.why: Prices often overshoot on news or panic and then partially return toward their average. Waiting for the close back inside avoids catching a falling knife on the first day of a drop.
watch_out: In strong trends prices can "walk the band" for weeks; reversion signals against a powerful trend often fail.
Combining it with the 200-day filter (only bullish signals above the 200-day) is a common way to reduce bad signals.
Targets are modest: the usual goal is a move back to the middle band, not a new trend.
strategies.settings: 20-day simple average, bands at ±2 standard deviations.

strategies.name: Donchian Breakout
strategies.tagline: Alerts when a stock makes a fresh 20-day high or low.
how: The Donchian channel is simply the highest high and the lowest low of the previous 20 trading days, about one month.
When the price closes above the top of that channel, it has done something it hasn't done in a month. Breakouts like this are how many trends begin.
strategies.bullish: The stock closes above the highest high of the previous 20 days.
strategies.bearish: The stock closes below the lowest low of the previous 20 days.
strategies.why: This is the core of the famous "Turtle Traders" rules from the 1980s. New highs attract attention and buyers; trend followers accept many small false breakouts in exchange for catching the occasional big trend.
watch_out: Most breakouts fail. The strategy only works on average because the winners can be much larger than the losers.
It fires often, so it's noisier than the other strategies. Check the bigger trend before taking a breakout seriously.
Breakouts on earnings days can reverse quickly.
strategies.settings: 20-day channel of highs and lows, signal on the daily close.

strategies.name: RSI Oversold / Overbought
strategies.tagline: Measures whether a move has gone too far, too fast.
how: The Relative Strength Index (RSI) compares the size of recent up days with recent down days over 14 days, giving a score from 0 to 100.
Below 30 is called "oversold" (selling has been unusually strong), above 70 "overbought". The alert fires when RSI leaves these zones, which signals the pressure is easing.
strategies.bullish: RSI rises back above 30 after being below it.
strategies.bearish: RSI falls back below 70 after being above it.
strategies.why: Sharp one-way moves often exhaust themselves. Waiting for RSI to exit the extreme zone, rather than buying the moment it enters, filters out some of the moves that keep going.
watch_out: In a strong uptrend RSI can stay above 70 for a long time, so bearish signals are unreliable in strong trends (and vice versa).
Oversold can get more oversold: a stock in real trouble can bounce briefly and fall again.
Best used on stocks in a range or as a timing tool inside an established trend.
strategies.settings: RSI 14 (Wilder smoothing), levels 30 and 70.

strategies.name: MACD Crossover
strategies.tagline: Catches shifts in short-term momentum.
how: MACD is the difference between a fast (12-day) and a slow (26-day) exponential moving average. When it rises, short-term momentum is improving relative to the medium term.
A 9-day average of the MACD itself is the "signal line". MACD crossing above the signal line means momentum just turned up; crossing below means it turned down.
strategies.bullish: The MACD line crosses above its signal line.
strategies.bearish: The MACD line crosses below its signal line.
strategies.why: Momentum tends to change before price trends do. The crossover is a smoothed, objective way to spot that turn. Crosses that happen far below zero (bullish) or far above zero (bearish) are often considered stronger.
watch_out: In choppy markets MACD crosses back and forth frequently.
It's built from moving averages, so it lags: fast reversals can be over before it reacts.
The alert note tells you whether the cross happened above or below zero, which adds context.
strategies.settings: EMA 12 and 26, signal line EMA 9.

strategies.name: Golden / Death Cross
strategies.tagline: The classic long-term trend change signal.
how: Two averages are compared: the 50-day (medium term) and the 200-day (long term).
When the 50-day rises above the 200-day it's called a golden cross: recent prices are now stronger than the long-term trend. The opposite, the 50-day falling below the 200-day, is a death cross.
strategies.bullish: Golden cross: the 50-day average crosses above the 200-day average.
strategies.bearish: Death cross: the 50-day average crosses below the 200-day average.
strategies.why: It confirms that a change in trend has lasted long enough to show up in two slow averages. Rare signals, often reported in financial news, and useful as a big-picture regime indicator.
watch_out: Very slow: the signal often comes months after the bottom or the top.
Each stock gives only a few signals per year at most, so expect long gaps between alerts.
In range-bound markets the two averages can tangle and give false crosses.
strategies.settings: Simple moving averages, 50 and 200 days.

strategies.name: Supertrend
strategies.tagline: A trailing line that flips when the trend turns.
how: Supertrend draws one line on the chart. In an uptrend it sits below the price, a set distance away; in a downtrend it sits above it. The distance is three times the stock's average daily range (the ATR), so it gives jumpy stocks more room than calm ones.

The line only moves in the trend's direction: in an uptrend it can rise but never fall, like a trailing stop. When the price closes through it, the trend flips and the line jumps to the other side. That flip is the alert.
strategies.bullish: The stock closes above the Supertrend line while it was in a downtrend: the line flips below the price.
strategies.bearish: The stock closes below the Supertrend line while it was in an uptrend: the line flips above the price.
strategies.why: It is a trend follower with a built-in exit. Because the line ratchets up behind a rising price, it lets winners run and gives back only part of the move before calling the turn. Measuring the distance in ATRs means the same rule fits a quiet utility and a volatile chip maker.
watch_out: In sideways markets it flips back and forth, giving a run of small false alerts.
It is always either up or down, never neutral, so it will call a trend even when there isn't much of one.
After a gap through the line the price can already be far from it, so part of the move is gone.
strategies.settings: ATR over 10 days (Wilder's smoothing), line 3 ATRs from the middle of each day's range, signal on the daily close.

strategies.name: Volume Breakout
strategies.tagline: A fresh 20-day high or low, backed by heavy trading.
how: This is the Donchian breakout with one extra check. The price must close beyond the highest high (or lowest low) of the previous 20 trading days, as before.
But it only counts if that day's volume is at least 1.5 times the average of the previous 20 days. Heavy volume means many buyers (or sellers) took part, not just a quiet drift over the line.
strategies.bullish: The stock closes above its 20-day high on at least 1.5× its average 20-day volume.
strategies.bearish: The stock closes below its 20-day low on at least 1.5× its average 20-day volume.
strategies.why: Most breakouts fail, and the weakest ones tend to happen on light volume. Requiring real participation filters out a large share of the false starts, at the cost of fewer alerts. Big funds can't hide their buying: when they move in, volume shows it.
watch_out: Earnings days and index rebalancing days bring huge volume for reasons that have little to do with the trend.
Fewer alerts than the plain Donchian breakout, and it can miss trends that start quietly.
Crypto volume varies a lot between exchanges, so the volume check is rougher there.
strategies.settings: 20-day channel of highs and lows, volume at least 1.5× its 20-day average, signal on the daily close.

strategies.name: Relative Strength
strategies.tagline: Spots the stocks that start beating the market, and those that start falling behind.
how: Relative strength compares a stock with the market, not with its own past. Divide the stock's price by SPY's price every day and you get the RS line: when it rises, the stock is doing better than the S&P 500, whether both are going up or down. (Crypto is compared with bitcoin, commodities with the average of all 19.)

The alert fires when the RS line closes at its highest level in 3 months (63 sessions): the stock has just become a market leader. A close at a 3-month low means it has become a laggard. Only switches count, so a leader that keeps leading alerts once.
strategies.bullish: The stock's RS line closes at a new 3-month high, after its last alert was a 3-month low (or it had none).
strategies.bearish: The stock's RS line closes at a new 3-month low, after its last alert was a 3-month high (or it had none).
strategies.why: Momentum is one of the best-documented effects in finance: stocks that have beaten the market over recent months have tended to keep doing so for a while. Many professional investors also watch the RS line for a new high before the price makes one, as an early sign of buying.
watch_out: It says nothing about the market itself. In a falling market a stock can lead simply by falling less.
Momentum can reverse sharply, especially after a long run or when the market changes leadership.
It needs the benchmark's data; a run without it produces no alerts for this strategy.
strategies.settings: RS line = price ÷ SPY (stocks), ÷ bitcoin (crypto) or ÷ the equal-weight average (commodities); 63-session high or low of the RS line, signal on the daily close.

strategies.name: Buy the Dip
strategies.tagline: Buys a big stock after a sharp drop and sells into the bounce.
how: The idea is that large, established companies tend to recover after a sudden drop. The strategy watches each stock's highest close of the last 20 sessions and alerts the first time it closes 5% or more below it.

It only buys. The trade is closed by a profit target (+10% from the buy price) or a time limit (60 sessions), whichever comes first. While it holds a stock it ignores new dips in that stock, so the time limit always counts from the buy; after selling, the next dip can buy it again. It also needs a close back above the line before it can alert on the same stock again, so one long slide gives one alert, not a new one every day.
strategies.bullish: The stock closes 5% or more below its highest close of the last 20 sessions, for the first time in this dip.
strategies.why: Short, sharp drops in big companies often come from news that the market overreacts to, and the price partly snaps back. Selling at a fixed profit locks in those bounces, and in a rising market most dips do recover, which is why this rule shows a high share of winning trades.
watch_out: A drop can be the start of a real decline, not a dip. Without the time limit a losing position is kept until it recovers, which can take years or never happen; in the 15-year test some positions sat 50–80% down for years and tied up the money.
A high win rate hides the size of the losses: many small +10% wins can be wiped out by a few large losers sold at the time limit.
The test uses today's S&P 100, so companies that fell and left the index are missing. That flatters buying dips more than almost any other rule.
strategies.settings: Dip: a close at least 5% below the highest close of the last 20 sessions (today included). Exit: +10% take profit, checked against each day's high, or after 60 sessions. New dips in a stock already held are ignored. Try other values in the Strategy Lab.

strategies.name: Double Top / Bottom
strategies.tagline: Two tests of the same level that failed: a possible reversal.
how: A double bottom forms when a stock falls to a low, bounces, falls back to roughly the same low, and holds. It looks like a "W". The peak between the two lows is the neckline.
A double top is the mirror image, an "M": two peaks at about the same price with a dip in between. The pattern is only complete when price breaks through the neckline.
strategies.bullish: Double bottom: two lows within 3% of each other, at least 10 days apart, then a close above the high between them.
strategies.bearish: Double top: two highs within 3% of each other, at least 10 days apart, then a close below the low between them.
strategies.why: The second test shows that sellers (for a bottom) couldn't push the price lower than last time. Breaking the neckline confirms buyers have taken control. A common target is the height of the pattern projected from the neckline.
watch_out: Patterns are drawn by an algorithm here; real charts are messy and some detected patterns will look less clean than textbook examples.
Without the neckline break it is not a pattern yet. Alerts only fire on the break.
Failed breakouts that fall back through the neckline are common.
strategies.settings: Swing points use 5 bars on each side; lows/highs within 3%; neckline at least 4% away.

strategies.name: Head & Shoulders
strategies.tagline: A three-peak reversal pattern, one of the best known.
how: A head and shoulders top has three peaks: a left shoulder, a higher head, and a right shoulder at about the same height as the left. The line joining the two dips between them is the neckline.
The inverse version is upside down: three lows, the middle one deepest. It's a bullish reversal pattern.
strategies.bullish: Inverse head & shoulders: price closes above the neckline.
strategies.bearish: Head & shoulders: price closes below the neckline.
strategies.why: The right shoulder failing to reach the head shows that the trend is losing strength. The neckline break confirms the shift. Like other patterns, traders often use the head-to-neckline distance as a rough target.
watch_out: One of the most "seen" patterns, which also means people find it where it isn't. The detector requires the head at least 2% beyond both shoulders and shoulders within 5% of each other.
The neckline can slope; the alert uses the sloped line, not a horizontal level.
Rare signal: expect few alerts.
strategies.settings: Swing points use 5 bars each side; shoulders within 5%; pattern within 120 days.

strategies.name: Triangle Breakout
strategies.tagline: Price squeezing into a point, then breaking out.
how: A triangle forms when the highs and lows converge: highs get lower, lows get higher, or one side is flat. The range keeps narrowing as buyers and sellers reach a balance.

Ascending triangles have a flat top and rising lows, descending triangles a flat bottom and falling highs, symmetrical triangles slope on both sides. The alert fires when price closes outside the pattern.
strategies.bullish: Price closes above the upper line of the triangle.
strategies.bearish: Price closes below the lower line of the triangle.
strategies.why: Narrowing ranges mean volatility is compressing, and compression is often followed by expansion. The breakout direction tells you which side won the tug of war.
watch_out: Breakouts can be false and reverse back into the triangle.
Ascending triangles lean bullish and descending ones bearish, but either can break the other way.
Lines are fitted to the last few swing points, so the drawing is an approximation.
strategies.settings: Swing points use 4 bars each side, last 70 days, line fit through the last 2-3 swing highs and lows.

strategies.name: Deck Patterns (Live Rules)
strategies.tagline: The trading bot's live chart-pattern rules: up breakouts in an uptrend, no chasing.
how: The trading bot looks for the chart patterns in Fidelity's guide "Identifying Chart Patterns with Technical Analysis" (Kirkpatrick): double and triple bottoms, rectangles, triangles, wedges, inverse head and shoulders, cup and handle, bull flags and pennants, gaps, pipe bottoms and six reversal candlesticks. Each day it reads the last 290 daily candles, finds the swing points and fits the pattern's lines.

Only upward breakouts are traded. A pattern counts on the day a candle closes above its breakout line by at least 0.2 ATR (a fifth of a normal day's range). The bot buys at the next day's open with the guide's protective stop just under the breakout candle, and has no target: it sells on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days, so winners can run.

The live rules add three filters, all judged on the breakout day: the close must be above its 50-day average; the trade is skipped if the next open is more than 2% above the breakout close (no chasing); and four patterns that lost money in the tests are never traded (double bottom, cup and handle, pipe bottom, hanging man).
strategies.bullish: A chart pattern breaks out upward on a close above its 50-day average: buy at the next open unless it opens more than 2% higher.
strategies.bearish: Sell when the price hits the protective stop, or on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days.
strategies.why: Breakouts from a clean pattern often start a new move, and the 50-day filter keeps it to stocks already trending up. With no target, the trades that work can run for months while the 20-day-low exit cuts the ones that don't.
watch_out: About three trades in four lose, mostly small; the result depends on a few big winners, so skipping trades changes it a lot.
Pattern detection is mechanical: some patterns a person would draw are missed, and some found ones look odd.
The pattern list and settings were tuned on the same 2018-2026 S&P 100 data they were tested on, and that list contains only today's members.
strategies.settings: Daily candles, last 290 per day. Zigzag swings 1.5 and 3 ATR (ATR 14); equal prices within 0.75 ATR; patterns at least 2.5 ATR tall and 10 candles long. Breakout close ≥ 0.2 ATR beyond the line. Entry next open; stop under the breakout candle; exit on a close below the 20-day low. Filters: close above the 50-day SMA; skip if the open is > 2% above the breakout close; no double bottom, cup and handle, pipe bottom or hanging man.
strategies.exit_text: Each trade is bought at the next open and sold at the stop or on a close below the 20-day low.
strategies.source: From the trading bot project (its live rules). Its own test, S&P 100 2018-2026: +23.9% a year against SPY's +15.5-16.0%, worst drop −20.6%, beat SPY in 10 of 10 start dates. This page runs it on this site's own backtest (money split equally across open trades, no costs), so its numbers differ from the bot's.

strategies.tagline: Pattern breakouts, only in stocks closing above their 50-day average.
how: The trading bot looks for the chart patterns in Fidelity's guide "Identifying Chart Patterns with Technical Analysis" (Kirkpatrick): double and triple bottoms, rectangles, triangles, wedges, inverse head and shoulders, cup and handle, bull flags and pennants, gaps, pipe bottoms and six reversal candlesticks. This version adds one filter: the breakout day's close must be above the stock's 50-day average, so it only buys breakouts in stocks that are already trending up.
strategies.bullish: A chart pattern breaks out upward on a close above its 50-day average: buy at the next open.
strategies.bearish: Sell when the price hits the protective stop, or on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days.
strategies.why: Breakouts work better with the trend behind them: the 50-day filter skips the ones in stocks that are still falling.

strategies.name: Deck Patterns, Break-Even Stop
strategies.tagline: Pattern breakouts with a stop that follows the price and locks in break-even.
how: The trading bot looks for the chart patterns in Fidelity's guide "Identifying Chart Patterns with Technical Analysis" (Kirkpatrick): double and triple bottoms, rectangles, triangles, wedges, inverse head and shoulders, cup and handle, bull flags and pennants, gaps, pipe bottoms and six reversal candlesticks. Each day it reads the last 290 daily candles, finds the swing points and fits the pattern's lines.

Only upward breakouts are traded. A pattern counts on the day a candle closes above its breakout line by at least 0.2 ATR (a fifth of a normal day's range). The bot buys at the next day's open with the guide's protective stop just under the breakout candle, and has no target: it sells on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days, so winners can run.

This version moves the stop every day: it is reset to the latest close minus the starting risk (entry minus stop), so it can move up or down. Once it reaches the entry price it never goes below it again, so a trade that has gone well can't turn into a loss.
strategies.bullish: A chart pattern breaks out upward: buy at the next open.
strategies.bearish: Sell when the price hits the moving stop, or on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days.
strategies.why: The moving stop protects gains sooner, so more trades end in profit (32% won in the bot's test) and drops are smaller.
watch_out: The tighter stop cuts some of the big winners the plain version keeps, which is where most of the profit comes from.
Pattern detection is mechanical: some patterns a person would draw are missed, and some found ones look odd.
The pattern list and settings were tuned on the same 2018-2026 S&P 100 data they were tested on, and that list contains only today's members.
strategies.settings: Daily candles, last 290 per day. Zigzag swings 1.5 and 3 ATR (ATR 14); equal prices within 0.75 ATR; patterns at least 2.5 ATR tall and 10 candles long. Breakout close ≥ 0.2 ATR beyond the line. Entry next open; stop under the breakout candle; exit on a close below the 20-day low. Stop: close − starting risk, every day; never below the entry once it has reached it.
strategies.exit_text: Each trade is bought at the next open and sold at the moving stop or on a close below the 20-day low.
strategies.source: From the trading bot project (version 8). Its own test, S&P 100 2018-2026: +18.5% a year, worst drop −22.6%. This page runs it on this site's own backtest (money split equally across open trades, no costs), so its numbers differ from the bot's.

strategies.name: Pattern Trader
strategies.tagline: The bot's first pattern trader: five up patterns that made money in every test period.
how: The trading bot's older pattern detector finds swing points with a zigzag (a swing counts once price reverses 2 ATR), then looks for five up patterns that made money in all four of its test periods: ABCD, falling wedge, inverse head and shoulders, triple bottom and Gartley.

A breakout must close past the pattern's entry level by 0.1 ATR on at least 1.3 times the usual volume. It buys at the next open with the pattern's own stop. ABCD trades sell at the pattern's target; the others have no target and sell on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days.
strategies.bullish: One of the five patterns breaks out upward on strong volume: buy at the next open.
strategies.bearish: Sell at the pattern's stop, at the ABCD target, or (other patterns) on a close below the 20-day low.
strategies.why: It trades rarely and only the patterns with the best record, so it was in cash a lot: the smallest drop of all the bot's stock strategies (−12.5%).
watch_out: The five patterns were picked on the same 8 years they were tested on, so the record flatters them.
Very few trades per stock; many stocks never trade at all.
Harmonic patterns (ABCD, Gartley) depend on exact ratios, so small price differences change what is found.
strategies.settings: Daily candles, last 250. Zigzag 2 ATR (fine 1.2 ATR), ATR 14. Breakout ≥ 0.1 ATR past the level on ≥ 1.3× the 20-day volume. Entry next open; pattern stop; ABCD target, others close below the 20-day low.
strategies.exit_text: Each trade is bought at the next open and sold at the pattern's stop, at the ABCD target, or on a close below the 20-day low.
strategies.source: From the trading bot project. Its own test, S&P 100 2018-2026: +18.3% a year, worst drop −12.5%, beat SPY in 10 of 10 start dates. This page runs it on this site's own backtest (money split equally across open trades, no costs), so its numbers differ from the bot's.

strategies.name: Breakout Bot
strategies.tagline: New 20-day highs above the 200-day average, confirmed by Bollinger Bands.
how: The trading bot's first strategy, on the daily chart. It needs three things on the same day: the close is above the 200-day average, the close breaks above the highest high of the previous 20 days (the Donchian channel), and Bollinger Bands confirm it: the close is above the upper band, or the bands were at their narrowest in 6 months (a squeeze) within the last 10 days.
It buys at the next open with a stop 2 ATR below the entry and sells on a close below the lowest low of the previous 20 days. No target, no shorts.
strategies.bullish: A close above the 200-day average breaks a new 20-day high, above the upper Bollinger band or after a squeeze: buy at the next open.
strategies.bearish: Sell at the stop (2 ATR under the entry) or on a close below the 20-day low.
strategies.why: Breakouts out of quiet periods (squeezes) in stocks that are already in an uptrend are a classic way to catch the start of a strong move.
watch_out: The bot also checked 15-minute and hourly charts; this page uses the daily chart only, which did much worse in the bot's test (+9.1% a year instead of +17.7%).

strategies.name: 50-Day Rule (Live)
strategies.tagline: Your live Bitcoin rule: buy the cross of a rising 50-day, sell on a failed high.
how: Your Bitcoin rule from the trading bot. It buys when the daily close crosses above the 50-day average while that average is rising (higher than 10 days ago), at the next day's open (00:00 UTC). After a sell it waits for a fresh cross.

After the buy it tracks the highest high so far. A swing high below it (a day with a high above the 3 days before it, followed by lower days) is a lower high: the bounce failed, so it sells. strategies.name: Above the 50 & 200-Day
strategies.tagline: Hold while the price is above both its 50- and 200-day averages, otherwise cash.
how: The simplest of the bot's crypto rules. After a daily close above both the 50-day and the 200-day average it buys at the next open (00:00 UTC); after a close below either one it sells at the next open and waits in cash.
There is no stop and no target: the two averages do all the work. On Bitcoin it was in the market about a third of the time.
strategies.bullish: The close is above both the 50-day and the 200-day average: buy at the next open.
strategies.bearish: The close falls below the 50-day or the 200-day average: sell at the next open.
strategies.why: Crypto's worst crashes happen below the long averages. Staying out then kept it at 0% in 2022, while Bitcoin fell 64%. It was set up before looking at any trades, so it's the least tuned of the bot's rules.
watch_out: Late in and late out: it gives up the start of every rally and part of every drop.
In sideways markets the price crosses the 50-day back and forth, with several small losses in a row.
Its edge was against holding Bitcoin from 2021; over longer periods holding did better.
strategies.settings: Daily candles (UTC). SMA 50 and SMA 200 of the close. Buy at the next open after a close above both; sell at the next open after a close below either.
strategies.exit_text: Each trade is bought at the next open after a close above both averages and sold at the next open after a close below either.

strategies.name: 50-Day Rule, Long + Short
strategies.tagline: Your 50-day rule both ways: long on a rising 50-day, short on a falling one.
how: Longs follow the live 50-day rule: buy when the close crosses above a rising 50-day average; sell on a lower high, a close below the 50-day or the starting stop.

Shorts are the exact mirror, the same rule on the chart turned upside down: sell short when the close crosses below a falling 50-day average; cover on a higher low, a close back above the 50-day or the starting stop above the last swing high. One position at a time; it can flip from long to short at the same open.
strategies.bullish: Buy at the next open: the close crosses above a rising 50-day average. A short is covered on a higher low, a close back above the 50-day or its stop.
strategies.bearish: Sell short at the next open: the close crosses below a falling 50-day average. A long is sold on a lower high, a close below the 50-day or its stop.
strategies.why: It earns in both directions, so it can make money in bear markets too. In the bot's test the shorts alone lost money (−3.9% a year), but they cut the drops of the long-only version.
watch_out: Shorting crypto needs futures or margin, with funding costs this backtest doesn't include.
The short side alone lost money in the bot's test.
Built and tested on Bitcoin; here it runs on every coin in the list.
strategies.settings: As the live 50-day rule for longs; the mirror (prices × −1) for shorts. Lower high / higher low after 1 day. One position at a time.
strategies.exit_text: Each trade starts at the next open after the signal and ends at the next open after the rule's exit (a lower high or higher low, a close back through the 50-day, or the stop).

strategies.name: Top-Down Analysis
strategies.tagline: Trendlines on seven timeframes, from weekly down to 5 minutes. Alerts when the price crosses one.
how: Top-down analysis means reading a stock from the biggest picture to the smallest: first the weekly chart, then the daily, then the 4-hour and 1-hour, down to the 5-minute. Each timeframe gets its own trendlines, drawn automatically with the same rules as the Trendlines page.

The green (rising) line runs under the lows from the lowest point of the period and acts as support. The red (falling) line runs over the highs from the highest point and acts as resistance. When both are intact the price is squeezed between them; sooner or later it breaks out of one side.

The scan checks every S&P 100 stock and SPY every 30 minutes while the US market is open. When the price crosses the newest green or red line on one of the timeframes you picked, you get an alert. Each line alerts only once.
strategies.bullish: The price crosses above the newest falling (red) trendline on that timeframe: the resistance gave way.
strategies.bearish: The price crosses below the newest rising (green) trendline on that timeframe: the support gave way.
strategies.why: A trendline marks where buyers or sellers have stepped in several times. When it finally gives way, the balance has shifted, and traders often watch for the move to continue. Checking the bigger timeframes first tells you whether a break goes with the larger trend or against it.
watch_out: Alerts use the latest price, about 15 minutes delayed, while the candle is still forming. It can close back on the other side of the line by the end of the candle.
Short timeframes (30m, 15m, 5m) have many lines that break many times a day. Most of those breaks are noise, which is why they're off by default.
A break against the bigger timeframes (say, a 1-hour break up while the daily line points down) fails more often. The strength score counts how many bigger timeframes agree.
Trendlines are drawn by a fixed rule, not by a person. Another trader might draw them differently.
strategies.settings: Lines from the highest high and lowest low of each timeframe's window, swing strength 5, a line counts as broken when a candle closes beyond it. Weekly 300 bars, daily 250, 4H 400, 1H 500, 30m 600, 15m and 5m 1,500. Regular US hours only, data 15+ minutes delayed (Alpaca).
